strengths: The paper addresses an important privacy and copyright-related problem with a practical inference-time intervention that requires neither retraining nor weight modification.

GUARD's attractive-repulsive guidance formulation and its prompt-adaptive cross-attention variant are intuitive and reasonably original extensions of classifier-free guidance and prior fixed-token attenuation methods.

The evaluation covers verbatim and template memorization, two Stable Diffusion versions, several relevant baselines, three metrics, runtime, non-memorized prompts, and useful block/head/timestep ablations.

The strongest result is on SD v1.4 verbatim memorization: CA-in-GUARD reduces SSCD from 0.113 for the strongest listed prior baseline to 0.079 while retaining comparable CLIP and FID. The method also substantially improves SSCD on SD v2.0 template memorization.

The presentation is generally clear, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not erase information from model weights and cannot protect against white-box extraction.
weaknesses: The experimental model-selection protocol appears to tune hyperparameters and select the best configurations on the same memorized prompts used for final reporting. No held-out validation prompts or nested selection procedure is described. This creates substantial selection bias, especially because separate configurations are selected per method, setting, and metric.

The claimed attention 'attenuation' is technically questionable as written. Multiplying a pre-softmax logit by alpha less than one does not necessarily lower its attention probability: it increases a negative logit toward zero and can therefore increase its softmax mass. The paper neither restricts logits to be positive nor analyzes this behavior, so the central mechanism and terminology are insufficiently justified.

The evidence for the proposed mechanistic account is thin. Figures 1 and 6 appear to show representative prompts rather than aggregate analyses with uncertainty across the dataset. These examples do not establish that the reported attention patterns systematically distinguish memorized from non-memorized prompts or cause memorization.

The detector is presented as statistical outlier detection, with tau=3 given as an example, but the best verbatim configurations search tau values as low as 0.01-0.05 for CA attenuation and 0.1-0.3 for CA-in-GUARD. Such thresholds flag many merely above-average tokens, undermining the characterization of the intervention as spike-specific or surgical.

Evaluation is narrow in architecture and data scope: SD v1.4 and v2.0 share essentially the same latent-diffusion/U-Net design, and only 72, 143, and 96 preselected prompts are evaluated. Thus, claims of robustness across architectures and broad deployment relevance are overstated; there is no evidence on newer transformer-based or larger diffusion models.

The statistical reporting is unclear. The paper says confidence intervals are computed 'across four generations,' which suggests only four seed-level aggregate observations rather than prompts as independent units. FID is computed from only 288-572 generated images against 10,000 apparently unmatched LAION images, making its absolute values and uncertainty unreliable.

Results are less uniformly dominant than the prose suggests. For SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. has better best-SSCD performance than CA-in-GUARD (0.479 versus 0.517); for SD v2.0, CA-in-GUARD ties plain CA attenuation on best SSCD and sometimes trades away quality. Per-metric 'best achievable' plots also use different configurations and therefore do not demonstrate a deployable joint operating point.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the stated code location is blank, baseline search spaces are not reported, grid resolutions and selected hyperparameters are absent, and key details such as seeds, scheduler, exact checkpoints, guidance scale s, prompt split construction, and implementation versions are missing.

The non-memorized-prompt safety experiment evaluates only CA attenuation, not the full CA-in-GUARD method, and uses just 200 prompts. It therefore does not support the broader suggestion that the proposed mitigation can be applied universally without harming benign generations.

The limitations discussion is candid about white-box access but does not address adaptive black-box attacks, test-set-driven hyperparameter selection, the narrow model family, or the fact that reduced SSCD against one known training image is not evidence of preventing reproduction of other training examples. These issues prevent the current evidence from supporting the paper's strongest safety claims.

strengths: Originality/significance: GUARD offers a potentially useful inference-time formulation that combines repulsion from the standard conditional prediction with attraction toward an attention-modified prediction. The dynamic, prompt-dependent spike detector is a sensible extension of fixed EOT-token suppression and targets an important privacy/copyright problem.

Soundness: The experiments cover two Stable Diffusion versions, distinguish verbatim from template memorization, compare against several relevant inference-time baselines, and include ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, and alternative attraction targets.
Presentation: The main motivation and inference procedure are generally understandable, and the paper reports joint SSCD/CLIP/FID trade-offs rather than presenting memorization reduction alone.

Limitations/ethics: The paper appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not erase information from model weights and therefore cannot protect against white-box extraction. It also reports approximate compute consumption and evaluates attention attenuation on 200 nominally non-memorized prompts.
weaknesses: Soundness: Hyperparameters are tuned separately for every method and setting on the same prompts used for final reporting, with configurations additionally selected according to the reported target metric. There is no validation/test split, and the grid resolutions, number of trials, selected configurations, seeds, and corresponding baseline search spaces are absent. This creates substantial test-set selection bias, especially because GUARD has more tunable parameters.

Soundness: The proposed operation is not necessarily an attenuation. Multiplying a pre-softmax logit by 0<alpha<1 decreases a positive logit but makes a negative logit less negative, potentially increasing its post-softmax attention. The paper neither restricts the selected logits to positive values nor analyzes this behavior, so the claimed mechanism is technically under-justified.

Soundness: The detector is described as statistical outlier detection, yet the searched Z-score thresholds are as low as 0.01–0.05 for SD-v1.4 verbatim memorization, which can flag a large fraction of above-mean tokens rather than exceptional spikes. This weakens the characterization of the intervention as 'surgical,' and the paper does not report the number or identities of tokens selected.

Soundness: The claimed benefit of the full GUARD framework is limited and lacks the decisive ablations needed to establish its mechanism. There is no repulsion-only or matched-guidance-scale control. In Table 1, GUARD and CA attenuation have identical SSCD on SD-v2.0 template cases (0.193), and their template-v1.4 confidence intervals overlap substantially. Thus the proposed attraction–repulsion synergy is not convincingly isolated.

Soundness/presentation: Some headline claims contradict the reported results. Under the primary best-SSCD protocol, Han et al. obtains 0.479 on SD-v1.4 template memorization versus GUARD's worse 0.517, despite claims of consistent superiority on template memorization and state-of-the-art performance across settings. Several other differences are small or within overlapping intervals, making phrases such as 'by far' inappropriate.

Evaluation: Prompt inclusion is determined using an observed SSCD threshold above 0.7, but the paper does not clarify whether independent seeds were used for filtering and evaluation. Reusing outcomes or seeds would induce regression-to-the-mean and inflate the no-mitigation reference. Results are also confined to only 72, 143, and 96 selected prompts from one previously identified set.

Evaluation: The privacy/security claim is evaluated only for exact known prompts and four generations per prompt. There is no adaptive black-box extraction, prompt paraphrase or perturbation attack, seed-search analysis, worst-case success rate, or thresholded leakage rate. Mean SSCD therefore does not show that the method 'guards against generating any memorized training example.'

Evaluation: Image quality evidence is inadequate. FID is computed from only 288–572 generated images against 10,000 generic LAION images, making it strongly sample-size-sensitive and poorly matched to the prompt-conditioned distribution. CLIP captures alignment rather than perceptual quality, and the paper provides neither human evaluation nor even qualitative generated examples.

Statistics: The confidence-interval procedure is ambiguous—the captions say intervals are computed 'across four generations' despite the nested prompt/generation structure—and FID has no uncertainty estimates. Statistical significance is asserted for the non-memorized experiment without specifying a test or accounting for paired samples and multiple metrics.

Reproducibility: The appendix states that code is available but gives a blank URL. It omits exact chosen hyperparameters, grid points, guidance scale, prompt identifiers, random seeds, sampler/scheduler details, software versions, and sufficient implementation specifics for reproducing attention aggregation. The reported ranges alone are insufficient to reproduce the tables.

Generalization/significance: Evaluation is restricted to old U-Net-based SD-v1.4/v2.0 checkpoints and one memorization corpus. There is no evidence for modern transformer-based diffusion models, other datasets, or naturally encountered prompts. Moreover, universal safety on non-memorized inputs is tested only for CA attenuation, not the full CA-in-GUARD method.

Limitations/ethics: Although the white-box limitation is honestly disclosed, the discussion understates black-box risks. Since memorized information remains in the model and the method is only a sampling modification, an adversary may bypass it through altered prompts, repeated queries, alternative samplers, or direct use of the unmodified inference path; none of these threat-model limitations is evaluated.

strengths: Originality/significance: GUARD is a useful inference-time formulation combining repulsion from the ordinary prompt-conditioned prediction with attraction toward a modified, safer prediction. The prompt-adaptive cross-attention spike detector is a practically meaningful improvement over fixed EOT-token interventions.

Soundness: The paper evaluates both verbatim and template memorization on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and template memorization on v2.0, includes five baselines, reports trade-off curves rather than only a single operating point, and provides informative block/head/timestep and positive-target ablations.

Evidence: The strongest gains are substantial, particularly for SD v2.0 template memorization, where CA-in-GUARD reaches SSCD 0.193 versus 0.260 for Wen et al. and 0.356 for Ren et al. under the best-SSCD protocol. The method also offers favorable Pareto frontiers in most tested settings.

Presentation: The motivation, attractive-repulsive construction, and inference procedure are generally clear. Separating verbatim from template memorization exposes meaningful failures hidden by aggregate evaluation.
Practicality: CA attenuation has modest measured overhead, and batching the three conditioning streams makes the full method implementable without modifying model weights.

Ethics/limitations: The paper addresses an important privacy and copyright risk and appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not erase information from the weights or protect against white-box extraction.
weaknesses: Soundness: Hyperparameters are tuned separately for every model/memorization setting and the best configurations are reported on those same examples, with no validation/test split. Selecting configurations independently for SSCD, CLIP, and FID further invites test-set overfitting and weakens the claimed state-of-the-art comparison.

The image-quality evidence is insufficient for the central claim of preserving quality. FID is computed from only 288–572 selected-prompt generations against 10,000 broadly sampled LAION images; this content-mismatched, small-sample FID is difficult to interpret as realism or diversity. CLIP only measures coarse prompt alignment, and no human evaluation or qualitative output comparison is provided.

The proposed logit operation is technically problematic as written: multiplying selected attention logits by alpha below one does not necessarily attenuate their softmax probability when a selected logit is negative, and the intervention is not invariant to adding a constant to all logits. The paper neither establishes that detected logits have the required sign nor analyzes this issue.

Several claims overstate the tables. On SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. achieves lower best-SSCD than CA-in-GUARD (0.479 versus 0.517); on SD v2.0, adding GUARD leaves best SSCD unchanged and slightly lowers CLIP at that operating point. The claimed significant improvement over Ren et al. for v1.4 verbatim memorization is also unsupported by the overlapping reported intervals.

Statistical reporting is unclear. The paper says confidence intervals are computed 'across the four generations,' despite having 72–143 prompts per setting, and does not explain the sampling unit or account for prompt-level and seed-level variation. FID has no uncertainty estimate, and paired significance tests are absent.

Generalization is limited to two closely related, older U-Net Stable Diffusion checkpoints and 311 highly memorized prompts selected from one 500-prompt benchmark. There is no evaluation on SDXL, transformer-based diffusion models, another memorization dataset, adversarial prompt variants, or held-out prompts.

The universal-deployment evidence covers only plain CA attenuation on 200 purportedly non-memorized prompts, not the main CA-in-GUARD method. It is also unclear which SD v1.4 memorization-tuned hyperparameters were used, since verbatim and template settings use substantially different ranges.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: the stated code link is blank, exact grid values and selected configurations are missing, baseline search spaces are not reported, and important sampling details such as scheduler, guidance scale, seeds, and checkpoint identifiers are unspecified. The notation also alternates between a single global S(p) and layer-local online spike detection.

Overall, the idea is promising and the empirical trends are encouraging, but independent hyperparameter evaluation, a well-defined attenuation rule, stronger quality assessment, and fuller reproducibility are needed before the central robustness and quality-preservation claims can be relied upon.

strengths: Soundness: The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a practically useful inference-time intervention that does not require retraining model weights. The attractive-repulsive formulation is intuitive, and separating verbatim from template memorization reveals meaningful differences hidden by aggregate evaluation.

Evidence: The evaluation covers SD v1.4, v2.0, and a limited v3.0 setting; several competing inference-time methods; SSCD, CLIP, FID, and DINO metrics; and ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, samplers, step counts, schedules, and CFG scales. On the reported benchmarks, CA-in-GUARD generally offers a strong memorization-quality trade-off, especially for verbatim memorization on SD v1.4 and template memorization on SD v2.0.

Significance: A lightweight, prompt-adaptive mitigation mechanism could be useful when practitioners only have access to pretrained models. The explicit non-memorized-prompt experiment and runtime/memory measurements are valuable practical additions.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. The distinction between the abstract GUARD framework, CA attenuation, and CA-in-GUARD is understandable, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not remove information from model weights or protect against white-box extraction.

Originality: Dynamic per-prompt selection of attention positions is a useful refinement over fixed EOT/padding interventions, and the analysis suggests that fixed token rules transfer poorly between verbatim and template memorization. weaknesses: Soundness: The stated attenuation rule multiplies selected pre-softmax logits by alpha<1. This does not necessarily attenuate attention: a negative logit becomes less negative and can receive more softmax mass. Because softmax logits are only meaningful relative to other logits, the paper needs either a sign/shift-invariant intervention, a proof of the claimed effect under stated conditions, or empirical verification that every selected token's post-softmax mass actually decreases.

The mechanistic evidence is too limited for the broad causal narrative. Figure 1 appears to show individual or representative prompts, without aggregate distributions, uncertainty, detector precision/recall, or interventions establishing that detected spikes are memorization-critical rather than merely correlated. Moreover, the tuned Z-score thresholds are extremely small in some settings (e.g., 0.01–0.05 for SD v1.4 verbatim), despite the motivating example using tau=3. Such thresholds flag many merely above-mean tokens and undermine the characterization of the procedure as statistical outlier detection or 'surgical' mitigation.

Evaluation configurations are selected on the same benchmark examples on which results are reported, separately for every architecture/memorization setting and target metric. There is no held-out validation set, and baseline search spaces, grid resolutions, and tuning budgets are not documented. This creates substantial adaptive overfitting risk and prevents determining whether the reported advantage comes from the method or unequal hyperparameter selection.

The statistical evaluation is not sufficiently reliable. Only 72, 143, and 96 prompts remain in the main settings, with four images per prompt. The manuscript ambiguously says confidence intervals are computed 'across four generations' and does not explain whether prompt/seed dependence or paired comparisons are handled. FID is especially unreliable on only 288–572 generated images, is compared against a broad 10,000-image LAION reference rather than a clearly matched distribution, and has no uncertainty estimates.

Several claims overreach the evidence. The non-memorized evaluation uses only 200 vaguely sampled LAION prompts and tests CA attenuation, not the full CA-in-GUARD method; it therefore does not justify the claim that mitigation can be applied universally without knowing whether a prompt is memorized. The SD v3.0 study contains only 39 prompts selected at a lower SSCD threshold and does not adequately specify how the U-Net-oriented attention intervention was transferred to the transformer architecture.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The 'Code' line is blank, while exact checkpoints, seeds, prompt lists, baseline implementations, complete search grids, selected configurations, and SD v3.0 intervention details are missing. The reported 1,500 GPU-hour cost further makes code and precise configurations important. As written, independent reproduction and fair comparison would be difficult.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. Linear combinations of unconditional, positive, and negative denoising predictions are closely related to established classifier-free, negative-prompt, and compositional guidance techniques, but that literature is not discussed sufficiently. The strongest novelty is the adaptive attention heuristic rather than the broad GUARD formulation.

Ethics and limitations are only partly treated. The paper correctly acknowledges residual memorization in the weights, but it does not discuss adaptive black-box attacks, circumvention of the inference wrapper, false assurance from imperfect similarity metrics, or handling of potentially copyrighted/private benchmark images. These omissions matter because the motivating deployment claims concern privacy and copyright protection.

strengths: Originality/significance: The combination of prompt-adaptive cross-attention spike detection with attractive-repulsive guidance is a potentially useful inference-time approach. Separating verbatim and template memorization also provides a valuable perspective beyond prior evaluations. Soundness breadth: The experiments cover SD v1.4 and v2.0, a limited SD v3.0 extension, five baselines, several samplers and guidance settings, alternate DINO similarity measurements, component ablations, non-memorized prompts, and computational cost.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithmic decomposition, and distinction between the GUARD framework and its cross-attention instantiation are generally clear. Tables and Pareto plots expose several quality-mitigation trade-offs rather than reporting only one metric.

Limitations/ethics: The paper appropriately motivates privacy and copyright implications and honestly acknowledges that inference-time suppression does not remove information from model weights or protect against white-box extraction. This acknowledgement should not itself be penalized.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central attention operation is not mathematically an attenuation. Multiplying a selected pre-softmax logit by α in (0,1) lowers a positive logit but makes a negative logit less negative, potentially increasing its softmax probability. The paper neither constrains selected logits to be positive nor proves or measures that attention mass actually decreases after the intervention. This directly undermines the claimed mechanism and its interpretation as surgical attenuation.

Evaluation selection bias: Hyperparameters are tuned separately for every architecture, memorization type, method, and target metric, but no validation/test split is described. The reported best configurations therefore appear selected on the evaluation prompts themselves. Search discretization, selected values, and comparable search spaces for baselines are also absent. The sharply different ranges across regimes further mean deployment requires knowing in advance whether a prompt exhibits verbatim or template memorization.

The claims overstate the results. On SD v1.4 template memorization, CA-in-GUARD has worse best-SSCD performance than Han et al. (0.517 versus 0.479), and under best-CLIP selection it is also slightly worse (0.667 versus 0.662). On SD v2.0, CA-in-GUARD merely ties CA attenuation at best SSCD. These results do not support statements that the method dominates across settings or improves every metric and setting.

Quality evidence is weak. FID is computed from only 288–572 generations in the main regimes against 10,000 broadly sampled LAION images, despite the generated set being conditioned on a highly selected prompt distribution. Such small, distribution-mismatched FID estimates are unstable and do not cleanly measure realism or preservation of utility. CLIP measures prompt alignment but cannot establish perceptual quality or semantic preservation by itself; no human evaluation is provided.

Statistical reporting is unclear. The paper says confidence intervals are computed “across four generations,” without explaining whether prompts or seeds are the sampling unit, and gives no paired tests despite using common prompts. FID has no uncertainty estimate. Several claimed differences have overlapping intervals, while the text still describes them as improvements.

The evaluation tests only a curated set of already-known memorized prompts and benign perturbations. It does not test adaptive extraction attacks, paraphrases, alternative seeds, repeated-query selection, or whether an attacker can bypass the intervention. Consequently, evidence does not support broad language such as guarding against generating “any memorized training example.” The 200-prompt benign test is too limited to justify universal application without quality loss.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the “Code” line is blank. Exact hyperparameter grids and chosen configurations, random seeds, prompt/type assignments, image preprocessing, LAION reference-set construction, baseline implementation details, and complete DINO/FID procedures are not supplied. The reported 1,500 GPU-hour requirement makes these omissions especially consequential.

The spike detector is insufficiently validated. The main text motivates an outlier threshold around τ=3, whereas reported searches include values as low as 0.01, which flag many merely above-average tokens rather than statistical outliers. There are no detector precision/recall results, stability analyses across heads and seeds, or controls showing that detected positions correspond specifically to memorization rather than ordinary prompt conditioning.

Overall, the idea is promising and the empirical effort is substantial, but the non-monotone “attenuation” operation, evaluation-time hyperparameter selection, weak utility metrics, overstated conclusions, and missing reproducibility information prevent the evidence from supporting the central claims. These are material issues requiring a substantially revised evaluation and technical account, yielding a Reject rather than a borderline recommendation.

strengths: Soundness: The paper presents a coherent inference-time method and evaluates it against five relevant baselines across SD v1.4, v2.0, and an exploratory v3.0 setting. Results cover verbatim and template memorization, multiple similarity and quality metrics, Pareto frontiers, qualitative examples, and sampler, timestep, block, head, schedule, and CFG ablations. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/4b5320a78f4f4fccb282f97242e1d9c0/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Significance: Inference-time mitigation is practically useful when model retraining or weight modification is unavailable. CA attenuation has little measured runtime or memory overhead, while CA-in-GUARD remains substantially cheaper in memory than several baselines.

Originality: The prompt-adaptive attention-spike detector is a useful advance over fixed EOT-token interventions, particularly because the paper identifies different attention behavior for verbatim and template memorization. Combining an attenuated conditional prediction with repulsion from the original prediction is also an interesting general framework.

The main empirical result is promising: CA-in-GUARD obtains the best reported SSCD in the principal SD v1.4 verbatim experiment, the full-spectrum evaluation, and the exploratory SD v3.0 evaluation, while generally retaining competitive CLIP and FID.

Presentation: The manuscript is clear and well organized. The method, experimental selection protocol, trade-offs, and distinction between best-per-metric configurations are explained unusually explicitly, and the visualizations are legible and informative.

The limitations and impact discussions appropriately acknowledge that inference-time mitigation does not erase information from the weights and cannot defend against white-box extraction. The work addresses a meaningful privacy and copyright concern without presenting an obvious new ethical risk.
weaknesses: The claimed attenuation operation is not mathematically guaranteed to attenuate attention: multiplying a selected pre-softmax logit by an alpha below one increases that logit whenever it is negative. It is also not invariant to adding a constant to all logits, although softmax itself is. Subtracting a positive offset, masking, or scaling attention probabilities would provide monotone attenuation. This weakens the stated mechanism and should be analyzed empirically, including how often selected logits actually decrease.

Hyperparameters appear to be tuned and selected on the same memorized examples used for final reporting, separately for every architecture, memorization type, method, and target metric. No held-out validation split or nested selection protocol is described. Given the small filtered sets (72, 143, and 96 prompts) and broad searches, the reported best configurations may be optimistically biased.

The uncertainty protocol is unclear: the paper says that means and 95% intervals are computed across four generations, but prompts—not generations—are the natural independent units. Exact seed handling, pairing across methods, and the confidence-interval calculation are absent. FID is also estimated from only a few hundred generated images in the filtered experiments, making it noisy and sample-size biased; no uncertainty or repeated-run analysis is supplied for FID.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The code URL is blank, Table 2 provides continuous ranges rather than exact grid values, and important details remain ambiguous, including attention aggregation across queries, heads, blocks, and token padding; the precise computation and lifetime of S(p); baseline search spaces; and how CA attenuation is transferred to SD v3.0's transformer backbone.

The security evidence is average-case and narrow. Evaluation uses known memorized prompts and four samples per prompt, but does not test worst-case seeds, paraphrases or prompt perturbations, repeated-query extraction, adaptive attacks, or the probability that at least one query reproduces training data. Consequently, language suggesting that the procedure 'guards against generating any memorized training example' is stronger than the evidence supports.

The incremental benefit of the full GUARD construction over CA attenuation is mixed. For the best-SSCD configuration it provides only a small change on SD v1.4 template memorization and exactly the same SSCD on SD v2.0; quality metrics are not uniformly better. Since Eq. 5 can partly behave like reducing effective conditional guidance when the positive and negative predictions are similar, a matched lower-CFG or guidance-norm control is needed to isolate the claimed attractive-repulsive synergy.

The claim that mitigation can be applied universally without harming non-memorized prompts is supported only for CA attenuation—not CA-in-GUARD—on 200 LAION prompts. Broader out-of-distribution prompts, rare concepts, compositional prompts, and larger-scale testing are necessary before making this deployment claim. Overall, the contribution is promising and useful, but these soundness and reproducibility limitations keep it at weak accept rather than accept.
